en.ai_prompt: The obligation to mention the exodus from Egypt at night underscores the importance of remembering this pivotal event in Jewish history both day and night. The Mishnah, an early third-century compilation of Jewish oral laws, discusses this obligation in the context of the evening Shema prayer.

description.en: Nighttime serves as the setting for pivotal moments in biblical history, including God’s [covenant of the pieces](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.15.12?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with Abraham, Jacob’s [wrestling](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.32.23?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with the angel, the [plague](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.12.29?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of the firstborn, and the [splitting of the sea](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.14.20?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic sources emphasize the special value of Torah study at night, teaching that a “[thread of kindness](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.12b.8?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)” accompanies those who engage in it, and many communities observe the custom of studying Torah throughout the night of Shavuot. Sources of Jewish thought and liturgy also portray the night as a particularly fitting time for introspection, devotion, prayer, and revelation.

[Liturgical works](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Liturgy) contain set prayers to be recited at regular schedules, while works of Jewish thought stress the importance of integrating personal connection into prayer.

description.en: The haggadah is the classic ritual text that serves as the base and script of the Passover seder. en.prompt: Sages in the Mishnah debate whether the Exodus needs to be mentioned in prayer at night. This first codification of Jewish law from the early third-century presents two opinions on the matter.
en.ai_prompt: The obligation to mention the liberation from Egypt at night underscores the enduring significance of this foundational event in Jewish history. The Mishnah Berakhot discusses the debate and eventual acceptance of including the liberation in the evening Shema prayer, interpreting the phrase 'all the days of your life' to encompass nights.

description.en: The book of [Exodus](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus?tab=contents) recounts how, after hundreds of years of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, God miraculously frees the people through a process of [ten plagues](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/the-ten-plagues?tab=admin) and the splitting of the [Red Sea](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/splitting-of-the-red-sea?tab=admin). The [Passover](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/passover?tab=admin) holiday commemorates these events, and discussing the Exodus is a focal point of the Passover [seder](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/seder?tab=admin).
description.he: יציאת מצרים היא סיפור המתואר בספר שמות בתנ״ך, שבמהלכו יצאו בני ישראל באופן ניסי משעבודו של העם המצרי. הניסים המרכזיים המתוארים בסיפור הם עשרת המכות ששיאם במכת בכורות, וקריעת ים סוף אשר אפשרה לעם ישראל לברוח מהצבא המצרי לכיוון ארץ כנען. חג הפסח מהווה זיכרון ליציאת מצרים, וההגדה של פסח, אשר אותה קוראים בליל הסדר, דנה בהשתלשלות האירועים.

en.title: Daily Reminders of Leaving Egypt
en.prompt: The Jewish liturgy is full of reminders of the exodus from Egypt. The Mishnah, the first codification of Jewish law from the early third-century land of Israel, in tractate Berakhot records a discussion about where in the liturgy, precisely, to mention the Exodus.

description.en: Egypt (Mitzrayim) plays a central role in the Bible, named both as a land of refuge and a land of danger and subjugation, particularly in the Passover narrative. Egypt is complex, both as the birthplace of the Jewish nation and as the one place the Torah tells Jews not to live. Despite this, Jewish communities flourished in Egypt from antiquity until relatively recently.
description.he: למצרים תפקיד חשוב בתנ"ך, והיא מוזכרת בו גם כמקום מפלט וגם כארץ של סכנה ושעבוד, בייחוד בסיפור יציאת מצרים. עבור היהודים מצרים היא תסביך – מצד אחד זהו מקום לידתו של העם היהודי, ומצד שני זהו המקום היחיד שנאסר עליו לגור בו.

description.en: Hillel was one of the most influential of the early sages, active toward the end of the first century BCE and the beginning of the first century CE. Coming from Babylon to the land of Israel, he became famous for his scholarship and his patient and tolerant manner. Bolstered by his Davidic lineage, he served as *nasi* (president) of the [*Sanhedrin*](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/sanhedrin?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources) (judicial assembly).
description.he: הלל היה אחד החכמים הראשונים, ומהפורים והמשפיעים ביניהם. הוא הגיע מבבל כדי ללמוד עם שמעיה ואבטליון, ונודע מהר מאוד בשל חוכמתו בתורה ואופיו הסבלני והסובלני. היותו צאצא של בית דוד הייתה בסיס לכהונתו כנשיא בתקופת שלטונו של הורדוס.

description.en: Time is a concept that appears from the very beginning of the Torah, as the world's creation unfolds over seven days, each of which is divided into evening and morning. Sources throughout the Jewish textual tradition discuss how God and people sanctify time, different ways of relating to the passing of time, how time governs the performance of commandments, and how to make the most of one's time.

en.title: Discerning the Dawn
en.prompt: Without clocks or other timekeeping devices, ancient Jewish law relied in part on the light of the sun to determine the boundaries of night and day. In the Mishnah, the first codification of Jewish law, the rabbis debate the earliest and latest times for reciting the Shema prayer in the morning, using the changing colors of the morning light as guidelines.

description.en: Light, both physical and metaphorical, features prominently throughout the Jewish textual tradition. Among other instances, light is the first thing God creates in the book of Genesis, is a focus of the holiday of [Chanukkah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/chanukkah?tab=sources), and is a central concept in kabbalastic literature, representing divine emanations.

en.ai_title: The Timing of the Morning Shema
en.ai_prompt: The timing of the Shema is crucial, as it reflects the dedication to affirming God's oneness at specific times of the day. The Mishnah, the first codification of Jewish law from the early third-century land of Israel, Berakhot 1:2 presents the rabbinic debate on the precise timing for the morning recitation of the Shema, highlighting its significance even if recited outside the prescribed time.

description.en: The morning prayer service in Judaism—*Shacharit* in Hebrew—consists of four main sections: preparatory prayers and readings; the [Shema](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shema?tab=admin) and its blessings; the [Amidah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shemoneh-esrei?sort=Relevance&tab=admin); and the concluding sections. The Torah is read on Mondays, Thursdays, and Shabbat, as well as on most other special days. Rabbinic sources delve into the origins and significance of daily morning prayers.
description.he: שחרית היא תפילת הבוקר. בתפילה זו כלולים ארבעה חלקים עיקריים: קטעי הכנה וקריאה מקדימים, קריאת שמע וברכותיה, תפילת עמידה (שמונה־עשרה) וקטעי סיום. התורה נקראת בימים שני וחמישי, בשבת ובמועדים.
